solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Idiot returns to sample tart

indicators.note: returns says the word for the idiot comes back, read from right to left

parts.note: a sap is a fool or idiot
to try something is to sample it

explanation.surface: A fool goes back to the baker's counter for another taste of a tart.
explanation.definitionFit: A tart is a baked case of this dough with a filling, so the pastry stands for the whole item.

clue.text: Vicar's average child

parts.note: par is the normal or average level
a son is a male child

explanation.surface: A clergyman's offspring is described as thoroughly ordinary.
explanation.definitionFit: A parson is a parish priest in the Church of England, the same office as a vicar.

clue.text: Perhaps put down rooks in corners, for example?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to set chess pieces such as rooks on the board
second meaning: in football, corners and free kicks are ..., rehearsed plays from a dead ball

explanation.walkthrough: Rooks sit in the corners of a chessboard, so the surface reads as one chess set-up; the corners are really football's.
explanation.definitionFit: Arranging chessmen is literally setting pieces, while in football a set piece is a planned move from a stoppage such as a corner kick.

clue.text: Speak highly of not beginning pay increase

indicators.note: not beginning says the word loses its first letter

parts.note: to praise someone is to speak highly of them

explanation.surface: A boss compliments a worker rather than giving more money.
explanation.definitionFit: A raise is the usual American term for an increase in salary, a rise in British usage.

clue.text: Cope with it being muddled, like much of Shakespeare!

indicators.note: being muddled says the letters of the two words are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone struggles to manage while confused, as so many characters do in Shakespeare's plays.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's plays are largely written in verse, so much of his work is in the form of poetry.

clue.text: Former marine ultimately boards punctually

indicators.note: boards says the letter gets on inside, as a passenger boards a ship

parts.note: to be punctual is to be on time

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of marine

explanation.surface: An ex-marine gets aboard right on schedule.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-time champion is a former champion, so the adjective means previous or erstwhile.

clue.text: Unfinished greenish-blue drink

indicators.note: Unfinished says the colour word loses its final letter

parts.note: teal is a dark greenish-blue colour

explanation.surface: A half-made drink of an odd blue-green colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea is the hot beverage brewed from leaves, a staple British drink.

clue.text: Animal is shy, old, and extremely tame

parts.note: coy means shy or bashful

indicators.note: extremely points to the two extreme letters of tame, its first and last

explanation.surface: A description of a timid, elderly and very docile creature.
explanation.definitionFit: The coyote is a wild North American member of the dog family, a type of wild beast.

clue.text: Treatment you're in store for?

parts.note: 'in store for' usually means awaiting you, but here it means literally inside a shop, where shopping itself is the cure

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'in store for' suggests something coming your way; read literally it means being in a shop.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase jokingly names shopping done to cheer oneself up, as though buying things were a medical cure.

clue.text: What a cat may get when eating small painting?

indicators.note: when eating says the cream phrase takes the letter inside, as food is taken in

parts.note: the cat that gets the cream is a proverbial picture of smug contentment
S is the clothing abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A puzzle about a cat's treat while it is having a snack.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'the cat that got the cream' gives THE CREAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Edvard Munch's famous expressionist work shows an anguished figure on a bridge; it is a celebrated picture.

clue.text: Chilling out initially near French city

indicators.note: near says the first piece sits right next to the next one
initially points to the first letter of out

parts.note: Nice is a city on the French Riviera

explanation.surface: Relaxing outdoors close to a city in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chilling out' looks like a phrase meaning relaxing; only 'Chilling' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Food or drink kept on ice is being chilled, so the phrase describes something being cooled.

clue.text: Man probing English prime minister's nickname

indicators.note: probing says the man's word goes into the middle of the others

parts.note: Pitt, Elder or Younger, was a British prime minister
he is the pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: A man digs into the nickname given to an English premier.
explanation.definitionFit: An epithet is a descriptive byname attached to someone, such as 'the Great', which works as a sobriquet.

clue.text: Holland's leader and Arab leader read out cordial greeting

indicators.note: leader points to the first letter of Holland
read out says the leader's title is said aloud, giving a word of the same sound

parts.note: a sheikh is an Arab chief or ruler

explanation.surface: The heads of the Netherlands and an Arab state meet and exchange warm words.
explanation.definitionFit: Clasping and shaking hands is a friendly salutation when people meet.

clue.text: Instruction from germophobe host? Confess everything!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a host fearful of germs would tell guests to arrive washed
second meaning: an idiom for telling the whole truth

explanation.walkthrough: The first reading takes the idiom literally, a host demanding clean visitors.
explanation.definitionFit: To own up fully and admit what you have hidden is the idiom's sense, while the literal sense is arriving washed.

clue.text: See alms distributed for illness

indicators.note: distributed says the letters are spread about into a new order

explanation.surface: Charity handed out to the sick, as though to cure a disease.
explanation.definitionFit: Measles is an infectious viral disease giving a red rash, common in childhood.

clue.text: Seamstress at first makes fun of garments

indicators.note: at first points to the first letter of Seamstress

parts.note: to mock is to make fun of

explanation.surface: A dressmaker initially ridicules some clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Smocks are loose overshirts or protective gowns, items of clothing.

clue.text: Criminal going around an unknown gorge

indicators.note: going around says the criminal's word surrounds the others

parts.note: a con is a convict, a criminal
Y is one of the letters used for an unknown quantity in algebra

explanation.surface: An outlaw wanders through an uncharted ravine.
explanation.definitionFit: A canyon is a deep, steep-sided valley, the same landform as a gorge.

clue.text: A thousand, I wager, is an error

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
a stake is the money wagered on a bet

explanation.surface: A gambler admits that betting a thousand was a bad idea.
explanation.definitionFit: A mistake is a slip or wrong act, a blunder.

clue.text: View through Downing Street?

indicators.note: Downing is read as swallowing, so the first word takes the other inside

parts.note: via means by way of, through

explanation.surface: A glimpse of the Prime Minister's London residence on Downing Street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Downing Street' is a famous London address, but 'Downing' here means gulping down.
explanation.definitionFit: A vista is a pleasing prospect or outlook, a scene seen from a point.

clue.text: Goddess has proven useful, in part

indicators.note: in part says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A deity has shown herself partly helpful.
explanation.definitionFit: Venus is the Roman deity of love and beauty.

clue.text: PC momentarily fixed for free

indicators.note: fixed says the letters are put right in a new order, as a broken computer is repaired

explanation.surface: A computer is repaired in an instant at no charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Complimentary tickets or drinks are given without payment, gratis.

clue.text: Silent parent

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to keep ... is to stay quiet
second meaning: a British word for mother

explanation.definitionFit: The word means saying nothing, as in 'keep it quiet', and is also the British informal word for one's mother.

clue.text: Island nation imports south Indian snack

indicators.note: imports says the nation takes the letter inside, as goods are brought in

parts.note: Samoa is an island country in the Pacific
S is the compass abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: A Pacific state brings in fried food from South Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: A samosa is a fried triangular pastry filled with spiced vegetables or meat, a South Asian savoury.

clue.text: Admiral, primarily unsmiling, is back on a ship?

indicators.note: primarily points to the first letter of Admiral

parts.note: stern means severe and unsmiling

explanation.surface: A grim-faced naval commander returns aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reads as returning; the definition means towards the rear of a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Astern means at or towards the rear of a vessel, a nautical word for behind.
